metadata.title: The claim that personality is more important than intelligence in predicting important life outcomes has been greatly exaggerated

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses six large representative longitudinal datasets (NLSY79, NLSY97, ADD Health, MIDUS, WLS, and OECD PIAAC 2012/PIAAC-L Germany follow-up) and applies listwise deletion based on success criteria. The paper does not report the use of complex survey weights or any specific weight variables (e.g., sampling/design weights) in the regression or correlation analyses, and it does not describe replicate-weight variance estimation. Because the analyses are based on correlations and R² from regressions (not PV-based ILSA scaling), the manuscript does not provide a PV/scale-weighting workflow typical of ILSA achievement reporting. Overall, the weighting strategy is not documented, so results should be interpreted as unweighted (or at least not transparently weight-adjusted) estimates of predictive validity within each dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses are conducted separately within each of the six datasets. The paper states that in all datasets it used listwise deletion depending on success criteria. For PIAAC, the authors analyze the original PIAAC 2012 sample (5465 participants) and the German follow-up longitudinal study (PIAAC-L; 3758 participants) because it includes supplementary Big-Five personality traits; participants are aged 16–65. For MIDUS, because the interest is educational and occupational success, the authors include only individuals below age 60 in the 2004–2006 wave.

main_findings.dataset_used: NLSY79 (1979 cohort; intelligence via AFQT; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.270; Personality = 0.029. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 9.3.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NLSY79 the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict educational attainment, finding that intelligence had far higher predictive validity than Big Five personality (R² 0.270 vs 0.029). This indicates that strengthening cognitive-skill development and using intelligence-like measures for educational selection may be more informative than relying on broad trait personality for predicting educational attainment, though the study is correlational and not causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: NLSY79 (1979 cohort; intelligence via AFQT; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.175; Personality = 0.011. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 15.9.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NLSY79 the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict high-school GPA, finding that intelligence substantially outperformed Big Five personality (R² 0.175 vs 0.011). This indicates that academic performance forecasting and interventions may benefit more from cognitive-ability measures than from broad self-reported personality traits, while recognizing that measurement reliability and construct validity differences can affect R² comparisons.

main_findings.dataset_used: NLSY79 (1979 cohort; intelligence via AFQT; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.target_variable: Log hourly pay (R² intelligence vs personality)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.148; Personality = 0.022. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 6.7.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NLSY79 the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict log hourly pay, finding that intelligence had higher predictive validity than Big Five personality (R² 0.148 vs 0.022). This indicates that workforce and earnings-related forecasting may be more strongly tied to cognitive ability than to broad trait personality, though the analysis remains non-causal and may be sensitive to how intelligence and personality are operationalized.

main_findings.dataset_used: NLSY97 (1997 cohort; intelligence via AFQT; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.328; Personality = 0.038. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 8.6.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NLSY97 the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict educational attainment, finding that intelligence strongly outperformed Big Five personality (R² 0.328 vs 0.038). This indicates that educational policy and guidance systems that aim to predict attainment may gain more from cognitive-ability information than from broad trait personality measures, while noting that the comparison is correlational.

main_findings.dataset_used: NLSY97 (1997 cohort; intelligence via AFQT; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.268; Personality = 0.020. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 13.4.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NLSY97 the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict GPA, finding that intelligence had much higher predictive validity than Big Five personality (R² 0.268 vs 0.020). This indicates that academic achievement prediction and targeted support may be better aligned with cognitive-skill measures than with broad personality traits, though construct and reliability differences between measures remain a caveat.

main_findings.dataset_used: NLSY97 (1997 cohort; intelligence via AFQT; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.target_variable: Log hourly pay (R² intelligence vs personality)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.096; Personality = 0.021. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 4.6.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NLSY97 the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict log hourly pay, finding that intelligence again exceeded Big Five personality (R² 0.096 vs 0.021). This indicates that earnings-related outcomes may be more effectively predicted using cognitive ability than using broad trait personality, while recognizing that the study does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: ADD Health (1994–1995 adolescents; intelligence via PPVT; success outcomes: educational attainment and log income)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.120; Personality = 0.064. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 1.9.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ADD Health the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict educational attainment, finding that intelligence still outperformed Big Five personality but by a smaller margin (R² 0.120 vs 0.064). This indicates that personality may have relatively more predictive value in some contexts, yet cognitive ability remains the stronger predictor for educational attainment in this dataset.

main_findings.dataset_used: ADD Health (1994–1995 adolescents; intelligence via PPVT; success outcomes: educational attainment and log income)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.031; Personality = 0.025. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 1.2.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ADD Health the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict log income, finding that intelligence only slightly exceeded Big Five personality (R² 0.031 vs 0.025). This indicates that for occupational/earnings outcomes in some adolescent-to-adult trajectories, personality traits may be closer in predictive validity to cognitive ability, though the analysis remains correlational and sensitive to measurement choices.

main_findings.dataset_used: MIDUS (1995 wave; intelligence via BTACT; success outcomes: educational attainment and log income; age restricted <60 in 2004–2006 wave)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.305; Personality = 0.061. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 5.0.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using MIDUS the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside age to predict educational attainment, finding that intelligence substantially outperformed Big Five personality (R² 0.305 vs 0.061). This indicates that cognitive ability remains a robust predictor of educational success even in adult samples, suggesting that educational policy should not over-weight broad trait personality when forecasting attainment.

main_findings.dataset_used: MIDUS (1995 wave; intelligence via BTACT; success outcomes: educational attainment and log income; age restricted <60 in 2004–2006 wave)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.091; Personality = 0.049. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 1.9.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using MIDUS the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside age to predict log income, finding that intelligence had higher predictive validity than Big Five personality (R² 0.091 vs 0.049). This indicates that occupational success forecasting may still benefit more from cognitive ability than from broad trait personality, while acknowledging that personality measurement reliability and construct validity can influence effect sizes.

main_findings.dataset_used: WLS (Wisconsin Longitudinal Study; intelligence via Henmon–Nelson; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.199; Personality = 0.079. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 2.5.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using WLS the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict educational attainment, finding that intelligence outperformed Big Five personality (R² 0.199 vs 0.079). This indicates that cognitive ability remains more predictive than broad personality traits for educational success in this cohort, supporting the use of cognitive measures in educational planning.

main_findings.dataset_used: WLS (Wisconsin Longitudinal Study; intelligence via Henmon–Nelson; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.245; Personality = 0.041. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 6.0.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using WLS the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict GPA, finding that intelligence strongly exceeded Big Five personality (R² 0.245 vs 0.041). This indicates that academic achievement prediction and interventions may be more effective when informed by cognitive ability rather than broad trait personality, while noting that the study does not establish causal pathways.

main_findings.dataset_used: WLS (Wisconsin Longitudinal Study; intelligence via Henmon–Nelson; success outcomes: educational attainment, GPA, log hourly pay)
main_findings.target_variable: Log hourly pay (R² intelligence vs personality)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.058; Personality = 0.079. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 0.7.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using WLS the study leveraged intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside gender to predict log hourly pay, finding an exception where personality had higher predictive validity than intelligence (R² 0.079 vs 0.058). This indicates that for earnings outcomes in some settings, broad personality traits may sometimes rival or exceed cognitive ability, but the authors report that this exception disappears when demographic controls are included.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 (Germany follow-up PIAAC-L; intelligence via averaged literacy & numeracy; success outcomes: educational attainment and log monthly income)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.168; Personality = 0.046. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 3.7.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 Germany (with PIAAC-L personality supplementation), the study leveraged averaged literacy/numeracy intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside age to predict educational attainment, finding that intelligence outperformed Big Five personality (R² 0.168 vs 0.046). This indicates that adult educational attainment is more strongly associated with cognitive competencies than with broad trait personality, supporting the prioritization of cognitive-skill development in adult learning policy.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 (Germany follow-up PIAAC-L; intelligence via averaged literacy & numeracy; success outcomes: educational attainment and log monthly income)
main_findings.target_variable: Log monthly income (R² intelligence vs personality)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (no controls): Intelligence = 0.057; Personality = 0.042. Ratio R² intelligence/personality = 1.4.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 Germany (with PIAAC-L personality supplementation), the study leveraged averaged literacy/numeracy intelligence and socioeconomic background (SEB) alongside age to predict log monthly income, finding that intelligence had higher predictive validity than Big Five personality (R² 0.057 vs 0.042). This indicates that occupational/earnings outcomes in adult populations are more closely linked to cognitive competencies than to broad trait personality, though the study remains correlational and measurement-dependent.

data.outcome_summary: This paper compares the predictive validity of intelligence versus Big Five personality for educational and occupational success using six representative datasets: NLSY79, NLSY97, ADD Health, MIDUS, WLS, and OECD PIAAC 2012 (with Germany’s PIAAC-L follow-up for Big Five traits). The authors do not apply machine learning; instead, they compute squared correlations (R²) and regression R² to quantify how much variance in outcomes is explained by intelligence versus personality, reporting ratios of R² as a relative-validity metric. Across datasets, intelligence shows substantially higher predictive validity for educational attainment and GPA (e.g., NLSY79: 0.270 vs 0.029; NLSY97: 0.328 vs 0.038; WLS: 0.199 vs 0.079), while occupational pay/income differences are smaller and sometimes show exceptions (notably WLS pay where personality exceeds intelligence without controls). Robustness checks include reliability correction and adding demographic controls (sex, age, SEB), which generally preserve intelligence’s advantage. Limitations include correlational design, potential construct validity/reliability differences, and the use of listwise deletion without transparent weighting documentation.
